name: Hydration / water chugging

lead: Some people drink very large volumes of water, sometimes gallons a day, hoping for plumper, glowy, clearer skin and a less puffy face. It is a common suggestion in skincare and appearance communities.

Proponents say more water hydrates skin from within. Skin hydration research looks at the barrier and outer layer, and the sources reviewed do not test drinking amounts. Reference sources say daily water needs vary with activity, age, health and climate, that the familiar eight-glasses advice is not scientific, and that thirst is a better guide than fixed targets. No trials of high water intake for facial appearance were found.

paras: People carry a large bottle and spread drinking through the day, often with a daily target, alongside a regular skincare routine. Some track intake with apps or marked bottles and watch their skin over weeks.
Drinking too much water too quickly can cause water intoxication and hyponatremia (low blood sodium), which can be fatal.

angle.text: Skincare and appearance communities suggest drinking large amounts of water, sometimes gallons a day, for plumper, glowy skin and less face puffiness. The idea is that skin is better hydrated from within. Trials of high water intake for facial appearance were not found.

lead: Hydration, or 'water chugging', is the habit of deliberately drinking large amounts of water through the day, sometimes a gallon or more, in order to look better: clearer, plumper, 'glowy' skin and a less puffy, more 'debloated' face. It is one of the most common appearance suggestions in skincare and looksmaxxing communities because it costs nothing, needs no products and fits into any routine.

Practitioners describe the chain as simple: skin that holds enough water looks fuller and smoother, and a body with enough fluid and electrolytes is said to hold less visible puffiness. Some community members instead emphasise sipping steadily and adding electrolytes or lemon rather than drinking large volumes at once.[1]

Reference sources describe daily water needs as varying with activity, age, health and climate, and note that the familiar 'eight glasses a day' figure is not a scientific rule, with thirst serving as a practical guide.[2][3] A 2018 systematic review of studies in healthy adults found that extra water intake was associated with a slight increase in skin hydration, mainly in people who previously drank little, while describing the evidence as limited in quantity and quality.[4] Drinking very large volumes quickly is associated with water intoxication and hyponatremia.[2][5][6]
infobox: Clearer, more hydrated-looking skin; less facial puffiness
Carrying a bottle, daily gallon targets, sipping with electrolytes or lemon
Roughly 0.8 to 1 L of water per hour in healthy adults[5]
Systematic review of 6 studies: slight rise in stratum corneum hydration with added water[4]

paras: Total water intake includes drinks and the water in food. Wikipedia reports US adequate intake levels of about 3.0 L for adult women and 4.0 L for men, with roughly 80 percent assumed to come from drinks, and European Food Safety Authority values of 2.0 L and 2.5 L, noting that needs rise with exercise and heat.[2]

In looksmaxxing and skincare circles the practice ranges from simply carrying a bottle to 'chugging' a gallon a day. Others refine the idea with electrolytes, lemon or slower sipping, on the theory that fluid balance rather than raw volume governs how the face looks.[1] The appearance goals are two: skin that looks hydrated (plump, even, 'glowy') and a face that looks less swollen or bloated, particularly in the morning or after salty meals.

The idea that people should drink a set number of glasses a day long predates online appearance culture. A 2002 review in the American Journal of Physiology by Heinz Valtin traced the familiar advice to drink eight 8-ounce glasses and searched for supporting studies. He reported finding none, noted that survey data suggested healthy adults in temperate climates with sedentary lives do not need such amounts, and that caffeinated drinks count toward fluid intake, while higher intakes are advisable in hot climates, with vigorous exercise or in certain diseases.[3]

A 2010 article in Clinics in Dermatology examined the advice specifically in relation to skin and reported finding no scientific proof for the recommendation of six to eight glasses for skin hydration, nor proof that drinking less is harmless.[7] Wikipedia's drinking water article describes the eight-glasses figure (about 1.9 L) as not scientific and thirst as a better guide than a fixed amount.[2]

In looksmaxxing and wider wellness communities the habit took a more intense form, with gallon-a-day targets, marked bottles and 'water chugging' framed as a free first step in a glow-up. Hacker News discussion of hydration research in 2023 likewise featured users reporting better focus, clearer skin and fewer headaches from drinking more water, which commenters themselves noted were self-reports.[8]

Skin is a barrier organ whose outer layer, the stratum corneum, holds water and limits loss through the surface. Laboratory studies measure transepidermal water loss and stratum corneum water content. One study found these measures change across the 24-hour day in healthy volunteers, and another found psychological stress, sleep deprivation and exercise altered barrier measures in healthy women.[9][10] These studies examine skin physiology rather than drinking amounts.

The most direct review is the 2018 systematic review in Skin Research and Technology by Akdeniz and colleagues. It identified 216 records, read 23 in full and included 6 studies of fluid intake and skin properties in healthy adults. The authors described the evidence as weak in quantity and methodological quality. Extra water intake was associated with a slight increase in stratum corneum and deeper skin hydration, mainly in people who previously drank less, with less dryness and roughness and slightly greater extensibility and elasticity. Effects on transepidermal water loss, sebum and skin pH were unclear, the mechanism was unknown, and the authors called for research on whether more fluid reduces signs of dry skin.[4]

Oral collagen supplements, a different route to hydrated-looking skin, have been reviewed in several meta-analyses. A 2021 meta-analysis of 19 trials reported favourable results for hydrolyzed collagen on skin outcomes, a 2023 analysis of 26 trials with 1,721 participants reported improved hydration and elasticity compared with placebo, and another 2025 analysis of 10 trials reported higher hydration scores. A 2025 analysis that separated trials by funding source and quality reported no effect among independent, high-quality trials.[11][12][13][14] These are studies of a supplement, not of drinking water.

Community accounts of water and facial puffiness point in two directions. Some members treat low water intake as a cause of a puffy, dull look and drink more; others report the opposite. One looksmax.org poster who described himself as prone to bloating wrote that he looked more 'debloated' after roughly halving the water he chugged, adding lemon and sipping in small, constant amounts, and asked whether heavy water intake might flush electrolytes. A reply in the thread endorsed spacing out each glass over thirty minutes to an hour.[1]

Reference sources explain hydration in terms of both water and salts: Wikipedia notes that heavy sweating raises the need to replace electrolytes, not just water.[2] Hyponatremia is defined as blood sodium below 135 mmol/L.[6] No published study has tested whether altering water intake changes facial puffiness in people without a medical condition.

Wikipedia's Dehydration article says thirst is normally an adequate guide to hydration for routine activities, that thirst can diminish with age, and that mild dehydration is associated with impaired cognitive performance at around 1 to 2 percent body-water loss.[15] Wikipedia's drinking water article says active people in hot climates may need 6 L a day or more.[2]

Studies of everyday hydration include a 2012 randomised trial in healthy young women in which mild dehydration produced by exercise changed mood and perceived task difficulty, and a 2016 randomised trial that compared how well different beverages maintain hydration status.[16][17] A 2010 review by Popkin and colleagues covered intake patterns, water balance, and links to energy intake, weight and performance, and called for long-term randomised trials.[18] A 2026 six-week study of 38 healthy adults given two 500 mL bottles of plain water a day found higher plain water intake and lower calorie intake at the end, with no significant change in urine specific gravity.[19]

A cohort study of serum sodium and biological ageing, shared on Hacker News under headlines such as 'Optimal hydration may slow down the aging process in humans', reported that higher middle-age serum sodium was linked to being biologically older; commenters questioned using serum sodium as a hydration measure, and the study's authors called for intervention trials.[8]

Common versions described in forums include a daily volume target (a gallon or a number of litres), a marked bottle with time points, sipping through the day, front-loading water in the morning, adding lemon or a pinch of salt or an electrolyte mix, and balancing water with salty foods. Some people treat clear urine as their marker; others, as in the debloating thread, reduce volume and focus on electrolytes.[1] Reference sources describe thirst, activity and climate as the usual determinants of need.[2][15]

Water intoxication is a potentially fatal disturbance of brain function caused by excess water intake that lowers blood sodium (hyponatremia). Early signs include headache, confusion, irritability and drowsiness; excess water moves into cells, raising pressure inside the skull, and severe cases involve seizures, coma or death.[5] Healthy kidneys excrete roughly 0.8 to 1 L per hour, and cases have followed drinking several litres within a few hours.[5]

Most reported deaths in healthy people have come from water-drinking contests or long exercise sessions with heavy fluid intake. Wikipedia cites a 2002 Boston Marathon study in which about 13 percent of finishers had hyponatremia and weight gain during the race was the strongest predictor, and describes the 2007 death of Jennifer Strange after drinking nearly 2 US gallons in a radio contest.[5] Hyponatremia is also associated with endurance events (about 10 percent of participants affected in one summary), certain medications, psychogenic polydipsia and hospital care.[6]

Symptom severity depends on how fast sodium falls, and a gradual drop is often better tolerated.[6] Wikipedia's drinking water article states that drinking too much too quickly causes these conditions.[2]

Hydration sits alongside humectant and barrier-focused skincare, oral collagen supplements, sleep and sodium management for morning puffiness, and electrolyte drinks. Hacker News and looksmax.org users frequently pair it with other glow-up habits.[1][8]

No studies found of high-volume water intake for facial appearance. Related research includes a systematic review of dietary fluid intake and skin hydration in healthy adults,[4] studies of skin barrier physiology,[9][10] trials of beverage hydration and mild dehydration,[16][17] and meta-analyses of oral collagen supplements.[11][12][13][14]

lore.intro: On looksmaxxing forums, water intake is discussed both as a basic glow-up habit and as a source of bloating, with some members experimenting with volume, timing and electrolytes.[1]

claims.claim: Drinking lots of water makes skin plumper and clearer.
Too much plain water causes facial bloating, and sipping with electrolytes looks better.
A gallon of water a day is the standard for a glow-up.
Eight glasses a day is required for healthy skin.
Drinking very large volumes quickly is harmless because the kidneys will flush the excess.
Collagen or electrolyte products boost hydration more than water alone.

timeline.event: A study in the Journal of Investigative Dermatology reports time-of-day variation in transepidermal water loss and stratum corneum hydration in healthy humans.[9]
A study in healthy women reports stress-induced changes in skin barrier function.[10]
Heinz Valtin reviews the evidence behind the 'eight glasses a day' advice; a Boston Marathon study finds about 13 percent of finishers with hyponatremia.[3][5]
Jennifer Strange dies after a radio-station water-drinking contest, becoming a widely cited case of water intoxication.[5]
Popkin and colleagues publish a review of water, hydration and health; a Clinics in Dermatology article examines eight-glasses advice for skin.[18][7]
A randomised trial finds mild dehydration changes mood in healthy young women.[16]
A randomised trial develops a beverage hydration index comparing drinks.[17]
Akdeniz and colleagues publish a systematic review of dietary fluid intake and skin hydration, including 6 studies.[4]
A serum sodium and biological ageing cohort study is widely shared and debated on Hacker News.[8]
Meta-analyses of oral collagen, including one split by funding source and study quality, report on skin hydration.[13][14]
A six-week study of 38 adults examines a daily increase in plain water on fluid and calorie intake.[19]
